name: IP masking (Private Relay, IP Protection, Tor)
plain: Some browsers route traffic through relays so sites do not see the visitor's real IP.
meaning: iCloud Private Relay (Safari, iCloud+ subscribers) uses two hops with a coarse egress location. Chrome IP Protection proxies selected third-party traffic in Incognito for known trackers. Tor routes everything over 3 hops.

web.api: OHTTP-style multi-hop relays; MASQUE; Tor circuits

steps: Browser sends traffic to a relay

limits.headline: Can see only a relay's address when you browse with Private Relay, IP Protection or Tor
limits.user_action: You turn on iCloud Private Relay, use Tor Browser, or browse in Chrome Incognito with IP Protection
can: See the relay's internet address instead of your home address
Guess your rough area from the coarse location a relay shares
Treat relay traffic as higher risk and ask extra questions or block it
cannot: Learn your real home address when the relay is working
Tell that a relay is in use with certainty, since a site can only guess from known relay lists
Get this from Firefox, which has no built in relay feature
Break the relay for you; the protection stays on until you switch it off
limits.differs: Private Relay is Safari with iCloud+; IP Protection is limited to Chrome Incognito and known trackers; Firefox has no built in relay.

story.what_it_is: Some browsers and services hide your real internet address behind a relay so sites see a different one.

marketing.name: iCloud Private Relay
marketing.pitch: Sends your browsing through two relays so no single party knows both who you are and which sites you visit.

marketing.name: Tor Browser
marketing.pitch: Bounces your traffic through volunteer servers so websites cannot see where you really connect from.

story.for_you: You usually notice nothing. Pages load as normal, but a site may think you are in a nearby city, not your own. Some sites may ask extra questions or block you because your address looks hidden.
story.for_makers: Makers see the relay's address, not the visitor's home address. That breaks easy location guessing, ad targeting by address and per-person rate limits. Teams must decide whether to trust, challenge or block these visitors.

use_cases.example: A Safari user with Private Relay on opens a news site. The site sees a shared regional address, so it shows a broad local edition, not street level local ads.
A player in a browser shooter connects through a relay. The game server sees a relay address, so matchmaking picks a server by relay region and ping can rise a few milliseconds.

Cloud gaming in the browser, such as Xbox Cloud Gaming or GeForce NOW, checks region before starting. A masked address can show the wrong country or add lag, so the player may be told the service is unavailable.
An ad network normally buys local ads by address. With masking, it only knows the broad area, so it falls back to page topic ads and reports less precise location data.
A bank sees a login from a relay address it has never seen. It may ask for a code by text, because relays hide the usual signals of where the person lives.
A store applies country pricing and tax by address. A masked visitor may see another region's price until they enter a shipping address at checkout.
A site counts unique visitors by address. Many people share one relay address, so the count is lower and the city report is blurrier.

technical_bounds: Only protects against sites, not the relay operator
Relay IPs appear on VPN lists and trigger blocks
Chrome IP Protection covers listed third-party domains only (reported)

value.abuse: Fraud and bot blockers treat relays as high risk

history.change: IP Protection roll out in Incognito (approximate, unverified)
